result: A novel bimanual stick manipulation task was developed where 72 participants manipulated a virtual stick (40 cm length, 15 cm hand separation) to reach targets with the stick tip. The task is kinematically redundant because the same tip position can be achieved with different stick angles, allowing investigation of both end-effector relevant (tip position) and end-effector irrelevant (stick-tilt angle) perturbations.
evaluation: Claims C4, C37-C47, and C176-C184 provide comprehensive methodological details including participant demographics (N=72, right-handed, aged 22.1±2.5 years), apparatus specifications (KINARM system, sampling at 1 kHz), and task parameters (stick dimensions, target distances, velocity feedback). The redundancy of the task is clearly established both conceptually and through the experimental design.

result: During baseline movements, participants consistently adopted a stereotypical strategy where stick-tilt angle was significantly modulated by tip-movement direction (|t(71)|>5.5, p<0.01), establishing a baseline TMD-STA relationship. This strategy minimized hand movement distance to near-optimal levels (Cohen's d=1.914 vs. parallel translation, d=0.334 vs. theoretical minimum), with clockwise tip movements accompanied by clockwise stick-tilt and vice versa.
evaluation: Claims C5, C48-C59, and C114-C122 are well-supported by statistical analyses (t-tests with Bonferroni correction, effect size calculations) and kinematic measurements shown in Figures 2-3. The stereotypical relationship is demonstrated from the first trials (C52) and quantified with appropriate statistical rigor. The optimization interpretation (C56, C119-C120) is supported by the distance minimization data.

result: In Experiment 1A (N=19), gradual 30° CCW tip-movement direction perturbation (1°/trial) led to implicit adaptation where participants corrected tip-movement direction (remained at baseline: t(18)=-1.320, p=0.203) by tilting the stick significantly more CW (t(18)=10.003, p<0.01). The adapted physical movement pattern followed the baseline TMD-STA relationship, resembling voluntary aiming at -30° target, with individual differences in stick-tilt correlated between baseline and adapted patterns (R=0.601, p=0.007).
evaluation: Claims C60-C72, C115, C129-C130, and C185-C187 are supported by appropriate statistical tests (paired t-tests, correlation analysis) and data shown in Figures 4-5. The gradual perturbation protocol ensured implicit adaptation (C62, C187). The finding that adaptation followed the baseline relationship is demonstrated both qualitatively (Figure 5b-c) and quantitatively (C69-C70, C72), though a small but significant difference in tip-movement direction was noted (C69).

result: Experiment 1B (N=13) with abrupt 30° tip perturbation allowing explicit strategy produced nearly identical results to Experiment 1A, but without the significant difference in tip-movement direction observed in Experiment 1A when comparing adapted pattern to baseline -30° target aiming.
evaluation: Claims C73-C75 and C188 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplements 2-3. The comparison between gradual (1A) and abrupt (1B) perturbation conditions provides important control data, though the sample size for 1B (N=13) is smaller than 1A (N=19). The absence of tip-movement direction difference in 1B (C75) contrasts with 1A (C74) and is appropriately documented.

result: The authors speculate that the residual tip-movement direction difference in Experiment 1A (but not 1B) was caused by implicit adaptation attempting to correct the abnormal visual stick-tilt angle, which would interfere with tip adaptation due to the baseline TMD-STA relationship constraint.
evaluation: Claims C76-C77 and C144-C145 are explicitly labeled as speculation by the authors. While the speculation is logical given the baseline TMD-STA relationship, it is not directly tested in Experiment 1. The authors indicate that Experiments 2 and 3 provide support (C145), but this remains an interpretation rather than a directly demonstrated mechanism.

result: In Experiment 2 (N=20), end-effector irrelevant stick-tilt perturbations (±6° around tip) that did not affect tip position were applied. Contrary to minimal intervention principle predictions, participants corrected stick-tilt angle from early adaptation (main effect of perturbation direction: F(1,18)=12.483, p<0.01), though not fully compensating for the perturbation (stick-tilt remained different from baseline: F(1,18)=54.457, p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C78-C89 and C189-C192 are supported by appropriate two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs comparing E2CCW and E2CW groups across trial phases. The statistical analyses properly test main effects and interactions. The finding contradicts minimal intervention principle (C83, C146) and is clearly demonstrated in Figure 7a-b. The perturbation magnitude (±6°) was appropriately chosen based on baseline data (C80).

result: Stick-tilt correction in Experiment 2 was accompanied by undesirable tip-movement directional errors (main effect: F(1,18)=5.104, p=0.037). These errors were consistent with predictions from the baseline TMD-STA relationship: CCW/CW stick-tilt adaptation shifted tip-movement in CCW/CW direction. Participants with shallower baseline TMD-STA relationships showed greater stick-tilt correction (R=-0.572, p<0.01), though correlation with tip-movement change was not significant (R=-0.440, p=0.052).
evaluation: Claims C90-C94 and C155-C158 are supported by statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA, correlation analyses) and data in Figure 7c-f. The finding that end-effector irrelevant adaptation produces end-effector relevant errors is novel and counterintuitive (C90, C155). The correlation analyses (C93-C94, C158) appropriately test individual differences, though one correlation approaches but does not reach significance (C94).

result: The combined results of Experiments 1 and 2 suggest implicit adaptation in the redundant task operates through two mechanisms: (1) the motor system attempts to correct any visual feedback perturbation regardless of end-effector relevance, and (2) physical movement correction patterns are constrained by the baseline TMD-STA relationship.
evaluation: Claims C95 and C116 synthesize findings from Experiments 1 and 2. The first mechanism is supported by Experiment 2 showing adaptation to end-effector irrelevant perturbations (C85-C89). The second mechanism is supported by both experiments showing adaptation trajectories following the baseline relationship (C68, C92). This synthesis is logical and well-supported by the experimental data.

result: Experiment 3 (N=20) investigated interactions between end-effector relevant and irrelevant perturbations by simultaneously applying CCW tip perturbation with either CCW (E3CCW, N=10) or CW (E3CW, N=10) stick-tilt perturbation. The E3CCW combination was predicted to align with baseline TMD-STA relationship enabling smooth adaptation, while E3CW was predicted to be orthogonal to the relationship potentially preventing smooth adaptation.
evaluation: Claims C96-C100 and C193-C195 describe the experimental design and predictions for Experiment 3. The design logically tests the interaction hypothesis derived from Experiments 1 and 2. The predictions (C98-C99) are clearly stated and based on the baseline TMD-STA relationship. Sample sizes are balanced between groups (N=10 each).

result: Contrary to predictions, final adapted movement patterns in Experiment 3 did not differ significantly between E3CCW and E3CW groups (tip-movement: t(18)=-0.479, p=0.638; stick-tilt: t(18)=-0.386, p=0.704). However, adaptation processes differed: trial-dependent trajectories were clearly separated (MANOVA group effect: F(8,162)=0.155, p<0.001), with E3CW showing more delayed tip-movement adaptation (trial segment 2: t(18)=-3.684, p<0.05). Trial-by-trial variability in latter adaptation phase also differed between groups (stick-tilt: t(18)=-3.235, p=0.005).
evaluation: Claims C101-C106, C117, and C160 are supported by appropriate statistical analyses (paired t-tests, repeated-measures MANOVA) shown in Figure 9. The finding that final patterns converged despite different trajectories is clearly demonstrated (C101-C102). The MANOVA appropriately tests multivariate effects across trial segments (C105). The delayed adaptation in E3CW (C106) supports the hypothesis that perturbation combinations affect adaptation dynamics even if final states converge.

result: The motor system's response to end-effector irrelevant perturbations (Experiment 2) is interpreted as predicting visual feedback of stick-tilt angle and attempting to eliminate dissociation between observed and predicted angles (sensory prediction error). This may reflect attempts to resolve vision-proprioception dissociation or utilize stick-tilt information to improve tip-movement direction estimation, given the tight coupling in the baseline TMD-STA relationship.
evaluation: Claims C146-C149 and C163-C168 present interpretations and speculations about mechanisms. While C146-C148 are supported by Experiment 2 data, the mechanistic explanations (C163-C168) are explicitly speculative. The sensory prediction error framework (C147) and multisensory integration perspective (C167-C168) are plausible but not directly tested. These remain interpretations rather than demonstrated mechanisms.

result: The baseline TMD-STA relationship plays a crucial role in both controlling movement of the redundant system and in how the motor system implicitly adapts to modify movement patterns. This relationship, developed through optimization, dictates physical control and informs visual feedback expectations. When perturbations occur, the motor system attempts to eliminate dissociations, but correction patterns are physically constrained by the baseline relationship, biasing adaptations toward this stereotypical relationship.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12 and C169-C175 synthesize the main conclusions across all experiments. The dual role of the baseline relationship (control and adaptation) is well-supported by baseline data (Figures 2-3) and adaptation experiments (Figures 5, 7, 9). The constraint on adaptation patterns is demonstrated across all three experiments. The framework (C175) integrating these findings is logical and supported by the data, though some mechanistic details remain interpretive.

result: The study addresses gaps in motor adaptation research by investigating redundant systems. Traditional non-redundant tasks (e.g., planar reaching) cannot examine how the motor system adapts by altering redundant body movement patterns. Previous studies on task-irrelevant perturbations applied perturbations to the end-effector, not to the redundant body while leaving the end-effector unaffected. The current study introduces a novel approach to investigate three problems: (1) coordinating redundant movements for end-effector control, (2) modifying redundant movements during adaptation to end-effector perturbations, and (3) responding to perturbations of redundant dimensions that don't affect the end-effector.
evaluation: Claims C1-C36 and C107-C128 establish the background, motivation, and novelty of the study. The characterization of traditional approaches (C1-C2, C16-C21) is accurate and well-cited. The identification of gaps (C3, C27, C32, C126-C128) is appropriate. The distinction between previous "task-irrelevant" perturbations and the current "end-effector irrelevant" perturbations (C35-C36, C111-C112) is clearly articulated and represents a genuine conceptual advance.

result: The bimanual stick manipulation task has several advantages: it creates redundancy naturally using a familiar everyday action (manipulating a stick with both hands), as evidenced by participants tilting the stick from the beginning of the experiment. The task allows investigation of how tip-movement direction perturbations lead to changes in both tip-movement and stick-tilt angle.
evaluation: Claims C113, C123-C125 describe advantages of the experimental design. The familiarity claim (C123-C124) is supported by Figure 2f showing immediate stick-tilting behavior. The acknowledgment of limited generalizability (C113) is appropriate given the specific configuration tested. The task's capability to investigate coupled changes (C125) is demonstrated throughout the experiments.

result: The finding that baseline movement patterns guide implicit adaptation is consistent with Hayashi et al., 2016, who showed that distorting the visuomotor map affected adaptation magnitude. The residual errors observed in visuomotor adaptation have been attributed to imbalance between learning and forgetting, though recent work (Albert et al., 2021) suggests the implicit learning system modulates error sensitivity based on error consistency.
evaluation: Claims C133-C135 and C141-C143 appropriately contextualize findings within prior literature. The comparison to Hayashi et al., 2016 (C133-C135) is apt and accurately represents that work. The discussion of residual errors (C141-C143) correctly cites relevant literature, though the connection to the current findings could be more explicit.

result: The adaptation pattern in Experiment 1A appears consistent with the minimal intervention principle because participants ignored abnormal visual stick-tilt that didn't directly influence the task. However, the difference between Experiments 1A and 1B implies a violation of this principle.
evaluation: Claims C139-C140 and C67 present conflicting interpretations about the minimal intervention principle. While C67 and C139 suggest consistency with the principle, C140 suggests violation. The evidence from Experiment 2 (C146) more clearly contradicts the minimal intervention principle. This apparent inconsistency reflects the complexity of the findings but could be more clearly resolved in the manuscript.

result: Previous studies created "task-irrelevant" conditions by manipulating cursor trajectory, target/cursor shape, or applying simultaneous perturbations to target and cursor, which are not "end-effector irrelevant" as defined in the current study. While some studies (Dimitriou et al., 2012; Omrani et al., 2013) used end-effector irrelevant perturbations in postural tasks, such perturbations have not been used to investigate motor adaptation patterns in redundant systems.
evaluation: Claims C150-C154 appropriately distinguish the current approach from previous work. The characterization of previous "task-irrelevant" manipulations (C150) is accurate and well-cited. The clarification that these are not "end-effector irrelevant" (C151) is conceptually important. The acknowledgment of exceptions (C152) and identification of the gap (C153) are appropriate.

result: Results from Experiment 3 support the existence of interaction between tip-movement and stick-tilt adaptation. If the motor system simply corrected stick-tilt to reduce sensory prediction error, the spillover effect on tip-movement would not have been observed. The motor system likely attempts to reduce both sensory prediction error and motor cost, given that the baseline TMD-STA relationship reflects motor cost minimization.
evaluation: Claims C159, C161-C162 present interpretations of Experiment 3 results. The interaction between adaptation types (C159) is supported by the separated trajectories and differential adaptation rates (C104-C106). The inference about dual optimization (C162) is logical given the baseline relationship reflects cost minimization (C119-C120), though this remains an interpretation rather than directly tested mechanism.

result: Data were analyzed using MATLAB R2023a with 10 Hz low-pass filtering (fourth-order Butterworth). Tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle were calculated relative to horizontal, with positive values indicating CCW direction. Values at peak tip velocity were used to evaluate feedforward motor commands. Statistical analyses included t-tests, correlations, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, and MANOVA.
evaluation: Claims C196-C202 describe data analysis methods. Software and filtering parameters are specified (C196-C197). Variable definitions are clear (C198-C200). The choice to use peak velocity values (C201) is appropriate for assessing feedforward commands. Statistical methods (C202) are appropriate for the experimental designs, though more details about multiple comparison corrections would strengthen reproducibility.
